```{r setup, include = FALSE, cache = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE,
                      fig.align = "center", fig.pos = "H", cache = TRUE, autodep = TRUE)
suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(network); library(sna); library(ergm); library(latentnet); library(coda)
})
options(knitr.kable.NA = "")

kab <- function(x, cap, align = NULL)
  knitr::kable(x, format = "latex", booktabs = TRUE, caption = cap, position = "H",
               align = align, row.names = FALSE, linesep = "", escape = TRUE)
pf <- function(p) ifelse(p < .001, "p < .001", paste("p =", formatC(p, format = "f", digits = 3)))
f2 <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 2)
f3 <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 3)
stars <- function(p) ifelse(p < .01, "**", ifelse(p < .05, "*", ""))

# Global options

set.seed(123)

N_CUG <- 1000   # CUG draws
N_QAP <- 1000   # QAP permutations
CC    <- c(CH = "Switzerland", FR = "France")
```

# Reproducibility

Replication data: \url{https://github.com/yasinshafi/508-problem-set-2} 

# Data

The data come from Metz and Brandenberger (2023), "Policy Networks
Across Political Systems," *American Journal of Political Science*
67(3): 569–586. The replication files are on the Harvard Dataverse. I
used the data for my ERGM tutorial.

In the original article, The authors surveyed actors in one policy
process -- emerging pollutants in water -- in four countries. I compare
two countries: Switzerland -- a consensus democracy, and France -- a
majoritarian democracy. The authors surveyed policy actors. Each
respondent checked the organizations it "closely collaborated" with. A
tie $i \to j$ means $i$ named $j$ as a close collaborator. The ties are
directed and binary.

The same survey asked each actor to name its opponents and to rate its
own policy beliefs and preferred policy instruments. I use these as
dyadic covariates:

-   **Opponent:** 1 if $i$ named $j$ as an opponent.
-   **Belief dissimilarity:** mean absolute difference over five
    core-belief items (1–4 scales).
-   **Instrument dissimilarity:** mean absolute difference over nine
    instrument items.

I also use two actor attributes from the paper's model: national
government (whether the sender or receiver was a national government
organization) and reputation (sender, and the absolute difference
between the two actors).

Only thise who responded in the survey appear in the networks. The
authors dropped non-respondents. Response rates were 89% in Switzerland
and 46% in France, so the French network covers a smaller share of its
policy field. This is a limitation for every method below. None of them
can recover ties to actors who are not in the data.

```{r data}
load("data/data_prepared.RData")   # collabXX, oppXX, attXX
load("data/attributeData.RData")   # attXX with imputed belief/instrument items

## ---- Helper: build a network object for one country ----------------------
## Collaboration matrix -> directed network, plus node attributes and the
## three dyadic covariates stored as network attributes.
make_nw <- function(collab, opp, att) {
  # Collaboration ties (no self-loops)
  m <- as.matrix(collab); diag(m) <- 0
  g <- network(m, matrix.type = "adjacency", directed = TRUE)

  # Node attributes
  g %v% "actorType"  <- as.character(att$actorTypesChar)
  g %v% "repuTarget" <- att$reputation

  # Dyadic covariate: opponent nominations
  o <- as.matrix(opp); storage.mode(o) <- "numeric"; diag(o) <- 0
  g %n% "O" <- o

  # Dyadic covariates: belief and instrument dissimilarity
  g %n% "B" <- dissim(att, 19:23)   # imputed core-belief items
  g %n% "I" <- dissim(att, 24:32)   # imputed instrument items
  g
}

## ---- Helper: pairwise dissimilarity ---------------------------------------
## Mean absolute difference between two actors across the given survey items.
dissim <- function(att, cols) {
  X <- as.matrix(att[, cols]); n <- nrow(X); M <- matrix(NA, n, n)
  for (i in 1:n) for (j in 1:n) M[i, j] <- mean(abs(X[i, ] - X[j, ]), na.rm = TRUE)
  M
}

## ---- Build the Swiss and French networks ----------------------------------
nw <- list(CH = make_nw(collabCH, oppCH, attCH),
           FR = make_nw(collabFR, oppFR, attFR))

## ---- Table 1: descriptive statistics --------------------------------------
desc <- data.frame(
  Country      = CC,
  Actors       = sapply(nw, network.size),
  Ties         = sapply(nw, network.edgecount),
  Density      = f3(sapply(nw, gden)),
  `Opponent ties` = sapply(nw, function(g) sum(g %n% "O")),
  `National gov.` = sapply(nw, function(g) sum(g %v% "actorType" == "national")),
  check.names = FALSE)
kab(desc, "The two collaboration networks", "lrrrrr")

```

The French network is less than half the size of the Swiss one but
almost three times as dense. Raw statistics such as transitivity rise
with density. So I compare each network with a null model that holds its
own size and density fixed, and I do not compare raw values across
countries.

# CUG test

**Question:** Are the networks more clustered and more centralized than
random networks of the same size and density?

I test two statistics. They match the paper's two hypotheses.

-   **Transitivity** (share of two-paths $i \to j \to k$ closed by
    $i \to k$). This is H2: Consensus democracies push actors to bargain and
    build broad coalitions. So H2 expects dense, close-knit collaboration, where
    an actor's partners also work with each other in Switzerland. Majoritarian
    democracies reward winning alone. So H2 expects sparser, more competitive
    ties in France. Higher transitivity relative to chance will support the
    consensus pattern.
-   **In-degree centralization** (how unequally incoming ties are
    spread). This is H1: power concentrated in a few actors. Consensus
    democracies spread power across many actors through federalism, 
    proportional representation and corporatist bargaining. So H1 expects
    incoming ties to be spread across several actors in Switzerland. Majoritarian
    democracies concentrate power in a few actors, often the national
    government.So H1 expects a few actors to receive most incoming ties in
    France. Higher centralization relative to chance supports the majoritarian
    pattern.

I use two null distributions. The first holds the number of ties fixed
(`cmode = "edges"`). The second also holds the number of mutual,
asymmetric and null dyads fixed (`cmode = "dyad.census"`). The second
null asks whether clustering goes beyond what reciprocity alone would
produce. Each null uses `r N_CUG` draws.

```{r cug}
## ---- CUG test statistics ---------------------------------------------------
## In-degree centralization (H1). Transitivity (H2) uses sna::gtrans directly.
icent <- function(g) centralization(g, degree, cmode = "indegree")

## ---- Helper: run one CUG test ----------------------------------------------
## Returns the observed value, null mean, 95% null range, the upper-tail
## p-value (share of null draws >= observed) and the raw null draws.
cug_one <- function(g, stat, mode) {
  set.seed(123)
  r <- cug.test(g, stat, cmode = mode, reps = N_CUG)
  c(obs = r$obs.stat, mean = mean(r$rep.stat),
    lo = unname(quantile(r$rep.stat, .025)), hi = unname(quantile(r$rep.stat, .975)),
    p = r$pgteobs, list(r$rep.stat))
}

## ---- Run all tests: 2 countries x 2 statistics x 2 nulls -------------------
## "edges":       random graphs with the same number of ties
## "dyad.census": same numbers of mutual, asymmetric and null dyads
cug <- list()
for (cc in names(nw)) for (st in c("Transitivity", "In-degree centralization")) {
  fn <- if (st == "Transitivity") gtrans else icent
  for (md in c("edges", "dyad.census")) cug[[paste(cc, st, md)]] <-
    c(cc = cc, stat = st, mode = md, cug_one(nw[[cc]], fn, md))
}

## ---- Table 2: CUG results -------------------------------------------------
## Obs./null scales the observed value by its own null mean, so the two
## countries can be compared despite different size and density.
cug_tab <- do.call(rbind, lapply(cug, function(x) data.frame(
  Country = CC[x$cc], Statistic = x$stat,
  Null = ifelse(x$mode == "edges", "Edges", "Dyad census"),
  Observed = f3(x$obs), `Null mean` = f3(x$mean),
  `Obs./null` = f2(x$obs / x$mean),
  `p (obs >= null)` = f3(x$p), check.names = FALSE)))
kab(cug_tab, sprintf("CUG tests (%d draws per null)", N_CUG), "lllrrrr")
```

```{r fig-cug, fig.width = 7.5, fig.height = 4.5, fig.cap = "CUG null distributions. Grey: ties held fixed. Blue: dyad census held fixed. The red line is the observed value."}

## ---- Figure 1: observed vs. both null distributions ------------------------
col_null <- c(edges       = adjustcolor("grey50", 0.5),
              dyad.census = adjustcolor("#0072B2", 0.45))
par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2.5, 1), oma = c(2.5, 0, 0, 0))

for (cc in names(nw)) for (st in c("Transitivity", "In-degree centralization")) {
  # Null draws under each conditioning
  e  <- cug[[paste(cc, st, "edges")]]
  d  <- cug[[paste(cc, st, "dyad.census")]]
  re <- e[[length(e)]]; rd <- d[[length(d)]]

  # Shared bins so the two nulls overlay cleanly
  xl <- range(c(re, rd, e$obs)); br <- seq(xl[1], xl[2], length.out = 40)
  he <- hist(re, breaks = br, plot = FALSE); hd <- hist(rd, breaks = br, plot = FALSE)

  # Overlaid histograms plus observed value
  plot(he, col = col_null["edges"], border = NA, xlim = xl,
       ylim = c(0, max(he$counts, hd$counts)),
       main = paste(CC[cc], "-", st), xlab = st, cex.main = 0.9)
  plot(hd, col = col_null["dyad.census"], border = NA, add = TRUE)
  abline(v = e$obs, col = "firebrick", lwd = 2)
  text(e$obs, max(he$counts, hd$counts) * 0.9, sprintf("obs = %.2f", e$obs),
       pos = 2, cex = 0.75, col = "firebrick")
}

## ---- Shared legend below the panels ----------------------------------------
par(fig = c(0, 1, 0, 1), oma = c(0, 0, 0, 0), mar = c(0, 0, 0, 0), new = TRUE)
plot(0, 0, type = "n", bty = "n", xaxt = "n", yaxt = "n")
legend("bottom", horiz = TRUE, bty = "n", cex = 0.8,
       fill = c(col_null, NA), border = NA, lty = c(NA, NA, 1), lwd = c(NA, NA, 2),
       col = c(NA, NA, "firebrick"),
       legend = c("Null: edges fixed", "Null: dyad census fixed", "Observed"))
```


```{r cug-nums}
cg <- function(cc, st, md = "edges") cug[[paste(cc, st, md)]]
r_tr <- sapply(names(nw), function(cc) cg(cc, "Transitivity")$obs / cg(cc, "Transitivity")$mean)
r_ce <- sapply(names(nw), function(cc) cg(cc, "In-degree centralization")$obs /
                                       cg(cc, "In-degree centralization")$mean)
```

**Results:** Both networks are more transitive and more centralized than
chance. The largest p-value across the eight tests is `r f3(max(sapply(cug, function(x) x$p)))`. Holding the dyad census fixed changes little. So the clustering is not just a by-product of reciprocated ties.

The size of the gap differs by country:

-   **Transitivity** is `r f2(r_tr["CH"])` times its null mean in
    Switzerland and `r f2(r_tr["FR"])` times in France.
-   **In-degree centralization** is `r f2(r_ce["CH"])` times its null
    mean in Switzerland and `r f2(r_ce["FR"])` times in France.

The CUG test points against H1. Relative to chance, the Swiss network is more centralized than the French one. But CUG conditions only on density. It cannot separate concentration of in-ties from reciprocity, closure or actor attributes. 

# QAP regression

**Question:** Are collaboration ties associated with opposition, belief
and instrument differences, and actor attributes?

I regress the collaboration matrix on the dyadic covariates with a
logistic network regression (`sna::netlogit`). The covariates are the
same exogenous terms as in the original paper's ERGM. Node attributes enter as
matrices: a sender matrix, a receiver matrix, or an absolute-difference
matrix. P-values come from `r N_QAP` permutations with Dekker's double
semi-partialling (`qapspp`). This method is robust to collinearity among
the covariates. The coefficients are ordinary logit estimates. QAP
corrects only their p-values for dependence among dyads.

```{r qap}
## ---- Helper: QAP covariate matrices ----------------------------------------
## Every predictor must be an n x n matrix. Node attributes are spread out:
##   sender effect   -> attribute repeated across each row    (matrix(x, n, n))
##   receiver effect -> attribute repeated down each column   (byrow = TRUE)
##   difference      -> |x_i - x_j|
qap_X <- function(g) {
  n <- network.size(g); nat <- as.numeric(g %v% "actorType" == "national")
  rep <- g %v% "repuTarget"
  list(g %n% "O", g %n% "B", g %n% "I",          # dyadic: opponent, belief, instrument
       matrix(nat, n, n),                         # sender is national gov.
       matrix(nat, n, n, byrow = TRUE),           # receiver is national gov.
       matrix(rep, n, n),                         # sender reputation
       abs(outer(rep, rep, "-")))                 # reputation difference
}

## ---- Term labels (same order as qap_X, plus intercept) ---------------------
qap_names <- c("Intercept", "Opponent", "Belief dissim.", "Instrument dissim.",
               "Out: national gov.", "In: national gov.", "Out: reputation", "Reputation diff.")

## ---- Fit QAP logistic regression for each country --------------------------
## qapspp = Dekker's double semi-partialling: permutes the residuals of each
## predictor, which keeps p-values valid when predictors are correlated.
qap <- lapply(nw, function(g) {
  set.seed(123)
  netlogit(as.sociomatrix(g), qap_X(g), nullhyp = "qapspp", reps = N_QAP)
})

## ---- Table 3: coefficients with stars, and two-sided p-values --------------
## pgreqabs = share of permutations with |b| at least as large as observed.
qap_tab <- data.frame(Term = qap_names,
  sapply(names(qap), function(cc) paste0(f2(qap[[cc]]$coefficients),
                                         stars(qap[[cc]]$pgreqabs))),
  sapply(names(qap), function(cc) f3(qap[[cc]]$pgreqabs)), check.names = FALSE)
names(qap_tab) <- c("Term", "Switzerland", "France", "p (CH)", "p (FR)")
kab(qap_tab, sprintf("QAP logistic regression (two-sided p from %d qapspp permutations; * p < .05, ** p < .01)", N_QAP), "lrrrr")
```

```{r qap-nums}
qp <- function(cc, k) qap[[cc]]$pgreqabs[k]; qb <- function(cc, k) qap[[cc]]$coefficients[k]
```

**Results:**

-   **Opponents:** Naming someone an opponent raises the odds of also
    naming them a collaborator. The effect is strong in Switzerland (b =
    `r f2(qb("CH", 2))`, `r pf(qp("CH", 2))`) and smaller in France (b =
    `r f2(qb("FR", 2))`, `r pf(qp("FR", 2))`).
-   **Beliefs:** Belief dissimilarity has no effect in Switzerland
    (`r pf(qp("CH", 3))`). In France it is negative but just misses the
    .05 level (b = `r f2(qb("FR", 3))`, `r pf(qp("FR", 3))`).
-   **Instruments:** Instrument dissimilarity lowers collaboration in
    both countries (`r pf(qp("CH", 4))` and `r pf(qp("FR", 4))`).
-   **Actors:** In France, national government actors receive more ties
    (`r pf(qp("FR", 6))`). In Switzerland, pairs that differ in
    reputation are more likely to be tied (`r pf(qp("CH", 8))`).

The QAP model treats each tie as independent once the covariates are
known. It has no terms for reciprocity, closure or popularity. 

# ERGM

**Specification:** I fit the authors' main model without the interaction
in each country. It has the covariates from the QAP model plus three 
endogenous terms:

-   `mutual`: reciprocity.
-   `gwesp(0.25)`: triadic closure (H2). Positive means ties form among
    actors who share partners.
-   `gwidegree(1.4)`: the in-degree distribution (H1). Negative means
    in-ties concentrate on a few actors.

I lengthen the MCMC interval to 5,000 to reduce autocorrelation.

```{r ergm}
## ---- ERGM specification (authors' main model, SI Table 4) ------------------
## %s is a placeholder for the in-degree term, so the same model can be refit
## with istar(2) as a robustness check.
##   edges                 baseline tie propensity (intercept)
##   edgecov("O")          i named j as an opponent           (H2: quality)
##   gwesp(0.25)           triadic closure                    (H2: density)
##   %s -> gwidegree(1.4)  in-degree concentration            (H1: power)
##   edgecov("B"), ("I")   belief / instrument dissimilarity  (H2: quality)
##   mutual                reciprocity
##   nodeofactor/ifactor   national gov. as sender / receiver
##   nodeocov, absdiff     sender reputation / reputation difference
ergm_rhs <- 'edges + edgecov("O") + gwesp(0.25, fixed = TRUE) + %s +
  edgecov("B") + edgecov("I") + mutual +
  nodeofactor("actorType", levels = "national") +
  nodeifactor("actorType", levels = "national") +
  nodeocov("repuTarget") + absdiff("repuTarget")'

## ---- Helper: fit one ERGM --------------------------------------------------
## Decay values (0.25, 1.4) follow the authors. A long MCMC interval (5,000)
## thins the chain to reduce autocorrelation between sampled networks.
fit_ergm <- function(g, deg = "gwidegree(1.4, fixed = TRUE)")
  ergm(as.formula(paste("g ~", sprintf(ergm_rhs, deg))),
       control = control.ergm(seed = 123, MCMC.interval = 5000))

## ---- Fit the main model in each country ------------------------------------
ergm_fit <- lapply(nw, fit_ergm)

## ---- Term labels (same order as the formula) -------------------------------
ergm_names <- c("Edges", "Opponent", "GWESP (0.25)", "GWI-degree (1.4)",
                "Belief dissim.", "Instrument dissim.", "Reciprocity",
                "Out: national gov.", "In: national gov.", "Out: reputation", "Reputation diff.")

## ---- Table 4: estimate, stars and standard error per country ---------------
## Columns of summary()$coefficients: 1 = estimate, 2 = SE, 5 = p-value.
ergm_tab <- data.frame(Term = ergm_names, sapply(ergm_fit, function(f) {
  s <- summary(f)$coefficients
  sprintf("%s%s (%s)", f2(s[, 1]), stars(s[, 5]), f2(s[, 2])) }), check.names = FALSE)
names(ergm_tab) <- c("Term", "Switzerland", "France")

## ---- Add BIC as a final row (used later to compare with istar(2)) ----------
ergm_tab <- rbind(ergm_tab, data.frame(Term = "BIC", Switzerland = f2(BIC(ergm_fit$CH)),
                                       France = f2(BIC(ergm_fit$FR))))
kab(ergm_tab, "ERGM estimates (standard errors in parentheses; * p < .05, ** p < .01)", "lrr")
```

**Convergence:** Table 5 summarizes the MCMC sample from the final
estimation round. A Geweke z-score beyond $\pm 2$ would signal that the
chain had not settled. Lag-1 autocorrelation shows how much each draw
depends on the last. The last column tests whether the simulated
statistics are centered on the observed ones.

```{r ergm-conv}
conv_row <- function(f) {
  sm <- as.matrix(f$sample)
  z  <- geweke.diag(as.mcmc(sm))$z
  ac <- apply(sm, 2, function(x) acf(x, lag.max = 1, plot = FALSE)$acf[2])
  dev <- colMeans(sm)   # sample is stored as deviations from the observed statistics
  c(`MCMC draws` = nrow(sm), `Max |Geweke z|` = f2(max(abs(z), na.rm = TRUE)),
    `Max lag-1 autocorr.` = f2(max(ac, na.rm = TRUE)),
    `Max |mean - obs| / SD` = f2(max(abs(dev) / apply(sm, 2, sd), na.rm = TRUE)))
}
ergm_conv <- data.frame(Country = CC, t(sapply(ergm_fit, conv_row)), check.names = FALSE)
kab(ergm_conv, "ERGM MCMC diagnostics (final estimation round)", "lrrrr")
```

Both models converged. No Geweke z-score exceeds 2, and the simulated
statistics sit close to the observed ones. Autocorrelation is moderate,
so I keep the long MCMC interval.

**Goodness of fit.** At the estimate, simulated networks reproduce the
model's own statistics by construction. So I check four statistics the
model was not fit to: the in-degree and out-degree distributions,
edgewise shared partners, and geodesic distances. Table 6 counts, for
each statistic, how many values fall outside the range of 100 simulated
networks and how many have a Monte Carlo p-value below .05.

```{r ergm-gof}
gof_terms <- ~ idegree + odegree + espartners + distance
gof_lab <- c(summary.ideg = "In-degree", summary.odeg = "Out-degree",
             summary.espart = "Shared partners", summary.dist = "Geodesic distance")
gof_count <- function(gf) sapply(names(gof_lab), function(k) {
  m <- gf[[k]]
  sprintf("%d / %d", sum(m[, "obs"] < m[, "min"] | m[, "obs"] > m[, "max"]),
          sum(m[, "MC p-value"] < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE)) })

ergm_gof <- lapply(ergm_fit, function(f)
  ergm::gof(f, GOF = gof_terms, control = control.gof.ergm(seed = 123)))

## Robustness: in-2-star in place of gwidegree (the authors' footnoted check)
ergm_istar <- lapply(nw, function(g) tryCatch(fit_ergm(g, "istar(2)"),
                                              error = function(e) conditionMessage(e)))
istar_ok   <- !sapply(ergm_istar, is.character)
gof_istar  <- lapply(ergm_istar[istar_ok], function(f)
  ergm::gof(f, GOF = gof_terms, control = control.gof.ergm(seed = 123)))

gt <- rbind(cbind(Model = "ERGM, gwidegree", Country = CC, t(sapply(ergm_gof, gof_count))),
            cbind(Model = "ERGM, istar(2)", Country = CC[istar_ok],
                  t(sapply(gof_istar, gof_count))))
colnames(gt)[3:6] <- gof_lab
kab(as.data.frame(gt), "ERGM goodness of fit: values outside the simulated range / values with MC p < .05", "llrrrr")
```

Fit is adequate in both countries. In France, no observed value falls
outside the simulated range. Shared partners and distances fit well in
both countries. The weak spot is the Swiss degree distribution. One
in-degree value and one out-degree value fall outside the simulated
range, and two in-degree values have small p-values. The model rarely
produces a hub like the Swiss actor that
`r max(degree(nw$CH, cmode = "indegree"))` of the other
`r network.size(nw$CH) - 1` actors name.

The authors report the same problem and use an in-2-star term as a
robustness check. I do the same. In Switzerland the `istar(2)` model has
a lower BIC (`r if (istar_ok["CH"]) f2(BIC(ergm_istar$CH))` vs.
`r f2(BIC(ergm_fit$CH))`) and fits in-degree better, but it misses one
shared-partner value. Its covariate estimates barely move (opponent
`r if (istar_ok["CH"]) f2(coef(ergm_istar$CH)[2])`, instrument
`r if (istar_ok["CH"]) f2(coef(ergm_istar$CH)[6])`).
`r if (!istar_ok["FR"]) "In France the in-2-star model is degenerate: the MCMC sampler does not mix. This is a known risk of Markov terms in small, dense networks, and it is why the curved term is the main specification."`

```{r ergm-nums}
ec <- function(cc, k) summary(ergm_fit[[cc]])$coefficients[k, 1]
ep <- function(cc, k) summary(ergm_fit[[cc]])$coefficients[k, 5]
```

**Results.**

-   **H1, power:** GWI-degree is negative in both countries: in-ties
    concentrate on a few actors. The coefficient is more negative in
    France (`r f2(ec("FR", 4))`) than in Switzerland
    (`r f2(ec("CH", 4))`). The authors find the same contrast with
    predicted probabilities. This is the pattern H1 predicts, and it
    reverses the raw CUG comparison.
-   **H2, closure:** GWESP is positive in both countries
    (`r f2(ec("CH", 3))` and `r f2(ec("FR", 3))`). This agrees with the
    CUG test.
-   **H2, opponents:** The opponent effect is positive and strong in
    Switzerland (`r f2(ec("CH", 2))`, `r pf(ep("CH", 2))`). In France it
    is smaller and not significant at .05 (`r f2(ec("FR", 2))`,
    `r pf(ep("FR", 2))`).
-   **H2, beliefs:** Belief dissimilarity matters only in France
    (`r f2(ec("FR", 5))`, `r pf(ep("FR", 5))`). In Switzerland it is
    null.

Coefficients are not strictly comparable across networks of different
size and density. Hence, the country contrasts show patterns of sign
and significance only.

# Latent space model

**Specification:** The latent space model (LSM) places each actor at a
point in a latent social space. The closer two actors are, the more
likely a tie between them. Closeness is transitive: if $i$ is near $j$
and $j$ is near $k$, then $i$ is near $k$. So the model captures
clustering without a closure term. I include the same covariates as in
the QAP and ERGM models.

I compared four specifications in each country by BIC and goodness of
fit:

-   latent dimension 1 or 2;
-   with or without sender and receiver random effects. These let each
    actor have its own tendency to send and to receive ties. The
    receiver variance measures how unequal popularity is, which relates
    to H1.

```{r lsm-select}
## ---- LSM covariates (same exogenous terms as QAP and ERGM) -----------------
## No gwesp or gwidegree here: the latent space absorbs clustering, and the
## random effects (when included) absorb degree heterogeneity.
lsm_cov <- '+ edgecov("O") + edgecov("B") + edgecov("I") +
  nodeofactor("actorType", levels = "national") + nodeifactor("actorType", levels = "national") +
  nodeocov("repuTarget") + absdiff("repuTarget")'

## ---- Candidate specifications ---------------------------------------------
## euclidean(d): tie probability falls with distance in a d-dimensional space
## rsender / rreceiver: actor-level random effects for sending / receiving ties
##   (receiver variance = how unequal popularity is, related to H1)
lsm_specs <- c("d = 1"                = "euclidean(d = 1)",
               "d = 2"                = "euclidean(d = 2)",
               "d = 1, sender/receiver" = "euclidean(d = 1) + rsender + rreceiver",
               "d = 2, sender/receiver" = "euclidean(d = 2) + rsender + rreceiver")

## ---- Helper: fit one LSM ---------------------------------------------------
fit_lsm <- function(g, spec, ctrl)
  ergmm(as.formula(paste("g ~", spec, lsm_cov)), control = ctrl, seed = 123)

## ---- Specification search -------------------------------------------------
## Shorter chains are enough to compare models; the chosen model is refit
## later with a longer chain.
sel_ctrl <- ergmm.control(burnin = 50000, sample.size = 4000, interval = 10)

## Fit each specification in each country, then record BIC and GOF counts
lsm_sel <- list()
for (cc in names(nw)) for (s in names(lsm_specs)) {
  m <- fit_lsm(nw[[cc]], lsm_specs[s], sel_ctrl)
  set.seed(123)
  gf <- gof(m, GOF = gof_terms, nsim = 100)   # same GOF statistics as the ERGM
  lsm_sel[[paste(cc, s)]] <- c(Country = CC[[cc]], Specification = s,
                               BIC = f2(summary(m)$bic$overall), gof_count(gf))
}

## ---- Table 7: BIC and GOF for each specification ---------------------------
sel_tab <- as.data.frame(do.call(rbind, lsm_sel), check.names = FALSE)
names(sel_tab)[4:7] <- gof_lab
kab(sel_tab, "LSM specification search. BIC (lower is better) and goodness of fit (values outside the simulated range / values with MC p < .05)", "llrrrrr")
```

In Switzerland, models without random effects leave observed values
outside the simulated range on most statistics. Adding sender and
receiver effects in one dimension leaves no observed value outside the
simulated range. That model also has the lowest BIC. In France every
specification fits, and BIC prefers the simplest model.

I use **one dimension with sender and receiver effects** in both
countries. It is the best model for Switzerland, and it fits France
well. Using one specification keeps the two countries comparable, as in
the ERGM.

**Estimation and convergence.** I run a longer chain for the final
models: 200,000 burn-in iterations, then 10,000 draws kept from every
50th iteration. Table 8 reports two checks on the coefficient draws and
the log-likelihood. The effective sample size (ESS) is the number of
independent draws the chain is worth. Geweke z compares the start and
the end of the chain.

```{r lsm-fit}
final_spec <- lsm_specs["d = 1, sender/receiver"]
fin_ctrl   <- ergmm.control(burnin = 200000, sample.size = 10000, interval = 50)
lsm_fit <- lapply(nw, function(g) fit_lsm(g, final_spec, fin_ctrl))

lsm_draws <- function(m) {
  b <- m$sample$beta; colnames(b) <- m$model$coef.names
  cbind(b, lpY = m$sample$lpY, receiver.var = m$sample$receiver.var)
}
lsm_conv <- data.frame(Country = CC, t(sapply(lsm_fit, function(m) {
  d <- as.mcmc(lsm_draws(m))
  ess <- effectiveSize(d); z <- geweke.diag(d)$z
  c(Draws = nrow(d), `Min ESS` = round(min(ess)),
    `Lowest-ESS term` = names(which.min(ess)),
    `Max |Geweke z|` = f2(max(abs(z))))
})), check.names = FALSE)
kab(lsm_conv, "LSM MCMC diagnostics (coefficients, receiver variance and log-likelihood)", "lrrlr")
```

```{r fig-trace, fig.width = 7.5, fig.height = 4.2, fig.cap = "LSM trace plots for the three dyadic covariates."}
par(mfrow = c(2, 3), mar = c(4, 4, 2.5, 1))
for (cc in names(nw)) {
  d <- lsm_draws(lsm_fit[[cc]])
  for (k in c("edgecov.O", "edgecov.B", "edgecov.I"))
    plot(d[, k], type = "l", col = "grey30", xlab = "Draw", ylab = "Value",
         main = paste(CC[cc], "-", c(edgecov.O = "Opponent", edgecov.B = "Belief dissim.",
                                     edgecov.I = "Instrument dissim.")[k]), cex.main = 0.9)
}
```

The trace plots show no drift. The largest Geweke z-score is
`r max(as.numeric(lsm_conv[["Max |Geweke z|"]]))`.
`r if (max(as.numeric(lsm_conv[["Max |Geweke z|"]])) <= 2) "All values are inside $\\pm 2$." else "One value is slightly above 2. With about a dozen monitored quantities, one such value is expected by chance."`
The smallest effective sample size is
`r min(as.numeric(lsm_conv[["Min ESS"]]))` draws.

```{r lsm-gof}
lsm_gof <- lapply(lsm_fit, function(m) { set.seed(123); gof(m, GOF = gof_terms, nsim = 100) })
lg <- data.frame(Country = CC, t(sapply(lsm_gof, gof_count)), check.names = FALSE)
n_out <- sapply(lsm_gof, function(gf) sum(sapply(names(gof_lab), function(k) {
  m <- gf[[k]]; sum(m[, "obs"] < m[, "min"] | m[, "obs"] > m[, "max"]) })))
lsm_gof_text <- if (all(n_out == 0)) {
  "In both countries, no observed value falls outside the simulated range on any statistic."
} else paste(sapply(names(n_out), function(cc) sprintf("In %s, %s observed value%s outside the simulated range.",
  CC[cc], ifelse(n_out[cc] == 0, "no", n_out[cc]), ifelse(n_out[cc] == 1, " falls", "s fall"))), collapse = " ")
names(lg)[2:5] <- gof_lab
kab(lg, "Final LSM goodness of fit: values outside the simulated range / values with MC p < .05", "lrrrr")
```

```{r fig-ideg, fig.width = 7.5, fig.height = 5, fig.cap = "In-degree fit for the ERGM and the LSM. The black line is the observed count. Points are simulated means and grey bars are simulated ranges."}
plot_ideg <- function(gf, main) {
  m <- gf$summary.ideg
  k <- as.integer(rownames(m)); keep <- k <= max(k[m[, "obs"] > 0]) + 2
  m <- m[keep, , drop = FALSE]; k <- k[keep]
  plot(k, m[, "obs"], type = "n", ylim = range(m[, c("min", "max", "obs")]),
       xlab = "In-degree", ylab = "Number of actors", main = main, cex.main = 0.9)
  segments(k, m[, "min"], k, m[, "max"], col = "grey75", lwd = 5)
  points(k, m[, "mean"], pch = 19, cex = 0.7, col = "#0072B2")
  lines(k, m[, "obs"], lwd = 2)
}
par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2.5, 1))
for (cc in names(nw)) {
  plot_ideg(ergm_gof[[cc]], paste(CC[cc], "- ERGM"))
  plot_ideg(lsm_gof[[cc]],  paste(CC[cc], "- LSM"))
}
```

The final LSM fits both networks. `r lsm_gof_text` On in-degree, the LSM
fits Switzerland better than the ERGM does (Figure 3). The receiver
effects let one actor be very popular without forcing the model to
change the whole degree distribution.

```{r lsm-tab}
lsm_names <- c("Intercept", "Opponent", "Belief dissim.", "Instrument dissim.",
               "Out: national gov.", "In: national gov.", "Out: reputation", "Reputation diff.")
lsm_ci <- lapply(lsm_fit, function(m) summary(m)$pmean$coef.table)
lsm_tab <- data.frame(Term = lsm_names, sapply(lsm_ci, function(t) {
  sig <- ifelse(t[, 2] > 0 | t[, 3] < 0, "*", "")
  sprintf("%s%s [%s, %s]", f2(t[, 1]), sig, f2(t[, 2]), f2(t[, 3])) }), check.names = FALSE)
names(lsm_tab) <- c("Term", "Switzerland", "France")
rv <- sapply(lsm_fit, function(m) m$sample$receiver.var)
sv <- sapply(lsm_fit, function(m) m$sample$sender.var)
vr <- function(x) sprintf("%s [%s, %s]", f2(mean(x)), f2(quantile(x, .025)), f2(quantile(x, .975)))
lsm_tab <- rbind(lsm_tab,
  data.frame(Term = "Sender variance",   Switzerland = vr(sv[, "CH"]), France = vr(sv[, "FR"])),
  data.frame(Term = "Receiver variance", Switzerland = vr(rv[, "CH"]), France = vr(rv[, "FR"])))
kab(lsm_tab, "LSM posterior means with 95\\% credible intervals (* interval excludes zero)", "lrr")
```

```{r lsm-nums}
lc <- function(cc, k) as.numeric(lsm_ci[[cc]][k, 1:3])
excl0 <- function(cc, k) { x <- lc(cc, k); x[2] > 0 | x[3] < 0 }
```

**Results.**

-   **Opponents:** The opponent effect is positive in Switzerland
    (`r f2(lc("CH", 2)[1])`). Its interval excludes zero. In France the
    estimate is positive (`r f2(lc("FR", 2)[1])`), but the interval
    includes zero.
-   **Beliefs:** Belief dissimilarity is null in Switzerland. In France
    it is `r f2(lc("FR", 3)[1])` with interval [`r f2(lc("FR", 3)[2])`,
    `r f2(lc("FR", 3)[3])`].
-   **Instruments:** Instrument dissimilarity is negative in Switzerland
    (`r f2(lc("CH", 4)[1])`). In France it is `r f2(lc("FR", 4)[1])`
    with interval [`r f2(lc("FR", 4)[2])`, `r f2(lc("FR", 4)[3])`].
-   **Popularity:** The receiver variance is `r f2(mean(rv[, "CH"]))` in
    Switzerland and `r f2(mean(rv[, "FR"]))` in France. Actors differ a
    lot in how often others name them, in both countries.

# Are the inferences robust?

Table 11 puts the three dyadic covariates and the national-government
receiver effect side by side across the three regression-type methods.
The estimates are on the log-odds scale in all three, but each
conditions on different things. QAP adjusts only the p-values for
dependence. The ERGM models dependence through explicit network terms.
The LSM models it through latent positions and actor random effects.

```{r compare}
cell_qap  <- function(cc, k) paste0(f2(qap[[cc]]$coefficients[k]), stars(qap[[cc]]$pgreqabs[k]))
cell_ergm <- function(cc, k) { s <- summary(ergm_fit[[cc]])$coefficients
  paste0(f2(s[k, 1]), stars(s[k, 5])) }
cell_lsm  <- function(cc, k) { t <- lsm_ci[[cc]]
  paste0(f2(t[k, 1]), ifelse(t[k, 2] > 0 | t[k, 3] < 0, "*", "")) }
terms <- list(Opponent = c(2, 2, 2), `Belief dissim.` = c(3, 5, 3),
              `Instrument dissim.` = c(4, 6, 4), `In: national gov.` = c(6, 9, 6))
cmp <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(terms), function(tn) { k <- terms[[tn]]
  data.frame(Term = tn,
             `QAP CH` = cell_qap("CH", k[1]), `ERGM CH` = cell_ergm("CH", k[2]), `LSM CH` = cell_lsm("CH", k[3]),
             `QAP FR` = cell_qap("FR", k[1]), `ERGM FR` = cell_ergm("FR", k[2]), `LSM FR` = cell_lsm("FR", k[3]),
             check.names = FALSE) }))
kab(cmp, "Covariate effects across methods. QAP and ERGM: * p < .05, ** p < .01. LSM: * 95\\% interval excludes zero.", "lrrrrrr")
```

**Robust results.**

-   **Instrument dissimilarity** lowers collaboration in both countries
    under every method. Actors work with those who prefer the same
    policy tools.
-   **The Swiss opponent effect** is positive and significant in all
    three models. Swiss actors collaborate with the actors they name as
    opponents. This supports the consensus-democracy part of H2.
-   **Belief dissimilarity in Switzerland** is null in all three models.
    Swiss actors collaborate across differences in core beliefs.
-   **Structure:** The CUG test, the ERGM's GWESP term and the LSM all
    point to strong clustering in both networks. The CUG test and both
    models also find unequal popularity.

**Results that depend on the method**

-   **The French opponent effect** is significant only in QAP. Once
    reciprocity and closure (ERGM) or latent positions (LSM) are
    modeled, it is no longer distinguishable from zero. QAP treats each
    tie as a separate observation given the covariates. Part of what it
    credits to opposition is carried by network structure.
-   **Belief dissimilarity in France** is negative in all three models.
    It is significant in the ERGM and the LSM, and just misses .05 in
    QAP (`r pf(qp("FR", 3))`). The direction is robust; the precision is
    not. With 18 actors, every French estimate is imprecise.
-   **National government in France** receives more ties in all three
    models. The effect is significant in QAP and the ERGM.
    `r if (excl0("FR", 6)) "In the LSM its interval excludes zero, but only barely" else "In the LSM its interval includes zero"`
    ([`r f2(lc("FR", 6)[2])`, `r f2(lc("FR", 6)[3])`]).
-   **Centralization (H1):** The CUG test finds Switzerland more
    centralized relative to chance. The ERGM finds a steeper
    concentration of in-ties in France. The LSM sides with the ERGM: the
    receiver variance is larger in France (`r f2(mean(rv[, "FR"]))` vs.
    `r f2(mean(rv[, "CH"]))`), though the intervals overlap. The methods
    answer different questions. CUG conditions only on density. The two
    models ask whether popularity is unequal once covariates and other
    network structure are accounted for. The H1 conclusion therefore
    depends on what one holds fixed.

**Summary:** The consensus-system findings for Switzerland are robust
across methods: collaboration with opponents, collaboration across
belief differences, and strong closure. The majoritarian-system findings
for France are weaker. The French network is small, and more than half
of the actors did not respond. The French opponent effect does not
survive models that account for network dependence.

cat(sprintf("Run with %s; %s.", si$R.version$version.string,
            paste(sprintf("%s %s", pk, sapply(pk, function(p) as.character(packageVersion(p)))),
                  collapse = ", ")))
